# AutoRnD-OS — technical-set-v2

**Set:** `evals/scenarios/technical-set-v2`
**Date:** 2026-09-26
**Why this set exists:** v1 was twenty variations of *distributed systems infrastructure* — DDL, pools, Kafka, K8s, CDN, tracing, SLOs. That is one subject area wearing twenty hats, and it meant the harness was never tested outside software operations (except `085`'s cup-sensor run, which passed). **This set is twenty genuinely different disciplines**, spanning physical, chemical, biological, structural, and regulatory domains, all producing a written engineering deliverable.

All twenty are **high difficulty**. There is no moderate band. Constraint shapes are deliberately varied — word bands, floors, caps, section counts, table counts, derivation counts, and mandatory calculations — so the classifier is exercised across branches rather than settling into one.

The item's trailing tag names what it exercises; the item itself does not announce it, because the planner is the thing under test.

---

## 1. Satellite end-of-life disposal

**`space-satellite-deorbit`**

A 1,240 kg satellite in a 780 km sun-synchronous orbit must be disposed of under a post-mission disposal requirement. It has 38 kg of remaining hydrazine and a delta-v budget of 148 m/s, with an estimated 11 m/s reserved for attitude control during the disposal phase. Its cross-sectional area is 6.8 m² and its ballistic coefficient is 78 kg/m². Earth's atmosphere at that altitude is highly variable and current solar flux is rising. Produce a disposal plan that derives the achievable orbit lowering from the available delta-v, states the re-entry interval with its uncertainty, identifies whether a controlled or uncontrolled re-entry is achievable, and quantifies the casualty-risk driver if the disposal underperforms. State which assumption dominates the uncertainty and how the plan changes if solar activity falls rather than rises. Between 1,100 and 1,350 words, exactly three sections, and must include a mass-and-delta-v budget table.

*Exercises: form/numeric (word band, 3 sections) · must-contain (budget table) · presence (ballistic coefficient, casualty risk)*

---

## 2. Somatic variant calling in a tumour sample

**`bio-variant-calling`**

A 1.2 TB whole-genome tumour-normal pair at 85× tumour coverage and 42× normal coverage must yield a somatic variant set for a clinical report. Tumour purity is estimated at 34% with ±6% uncertainty; the sample has a measured duplication rate of 18% and two sequencing batches with different error profiles. A known artefact is that 0.4% of positions show strand bias from a library-prep lot. Design the calling pipeline: the minimum evidence thresholds that account for purity, the filtering that removes the batch artefact without discarding true low-allele-fraction variants, the orthogonal validation strategy and what fraction of calls it must validate to be informative, and the reporting thresholds that a clinician can act on. Give the expected number of false positives at your chosen threshold and the arithmetic that supports it. The plan must not cite a published pipeline as the justification for a threshold. At most 1,400 words; must include ≥4 distinct numeric derivations.

*Exercises: prohibition (no published-pipeline appeal) · form/numeric (word cap, ≥4 derivations) · presence (purity, allele fraction, orthogonal validation)*

---

## 3. Seismic retrofit of an existing frame

**`civil-seismic-retrofit`**

A four-storey reinforced-concrete moment frame built in 1962 holds a hospital wing. It has non-ductile detailing, a fundamental period of 0.68 s, and a computed base shear that is 41% of the current code demand. Floor-to-floor height is 3.6 m; the wing is 32 m × 18 m in plan. A retrofit must keep the wing operational during construction. Evaluate at least two retrofit strategies, derive the target performance level and the drift limit you are designing to, and state how you would verify the existing foundation can accept the increased overturning. Identify the failure mode that no strengthening of the superstructure can fix. Between 1,200 and 1,450 words, at least 1,250; must describe exactly two figures and state that a drift check governs. Must not describe any approach as "proven" without naming the evidence.

*Exercises: form (word floor, exactly 2 figures, drift check) · prohibition (no "proven" without evidence) · presence (period, base shear, footing)*

---

## 4. Interconnecting an inverter-based resource

**`power-ibr-interconnection`**

A 180 MW solar plant with 45 MW / 180 MWh of co-located battery storage is interconnecting to a 230 kV transmission network with a short-circuit ratio of 2.1 at the point of interconnection. The network has one existing synchronous generator of 400 MVA. The utility has raised concerns about weak-grid behaviour, subsynchronous oscillations, and voltage ride-through during remote faults. Design the interconnection study: the electromagnetic-transient modelling required, the control settings that address the low short-circuit ratio, the ride-through envelope you commit to and why it is achievable, and the protection that detects an islanded condition the plant cannot see. Give the short-circuit ratio arithmetic and the point at which the plant must curtail. Present the three most likely study outcomes and what each would require. Under 1,300 words; must not name a manufacturer or a model number.

*Exercises: prohibition (no vendor names) · form/numeric (word cap, SCR arithmetic) · presence (ride-through, subsynchronous oscillation)*

---

## 5. Preventing thermal runaway in a batch reactor

**`chem-exotherm-runaway`**

A 12 m³ jacketed batch reactor runs a semi-batch nitration with a reaction enthalpy of −340 kJ/mol, a feed rate of 180 kg/h of a reactant with a molecular weight of 137 g/mol, and a measured accumulation of 22% under normal cooling. The cooling system provides 480 kW at a 15 K approach; the vessel's heat capacity is 3.1 kJ/kg·K and the charge mass before feed is 6,800 kg. Design the safety case: the adiabatic temperature rise derivation, the maximum temperature if cooling is lost at the worst point in the feed, the time to that maximum, the onset temperature of the decomposition you must stay below, and the instrumentation and interlocks that prevent reaching it. Identify the single parameter whose uncertainty most changes the verdict and state how you would bound it. At most 1,250 words, exactly four sections, and must contain the adiabatic-rise calculation explicitly.

*Exercises: form (word cap, 4 sections) · must-contain (adiabatic rise) · presence (accumulation, onset temperature, interlock)*

---

## 6. Hydrogen embrittlement in a welded pressure boundary

**`materials-h2-embrittlement`**

A 42 mm wall-thickness carbon-manganese steel vessel operates at 100 bar hydrogen and 320 °C with 1,400 thermal cycles to −20 °C over its design life. The welds are single-pass submerged arc with a measured heat-affected-zone hardness of 245 HV10, and the parent metal has a yield of 355 MPa. A fitness-for-service review must establish whether the vessel can continue for 15 more years. Evaluate the governing failure mode, state the material properties you require and why the ones you have are insufficient, give the fracture-mechanics calculation that bounds the remaining life, and specify the inspection that would actually find the damage mechanism you consider dominant. Name the two further tests you would commission and what each would change about the verdict. Between 1,150 and 1,400 words; must state at least three material properties with their units; must not dismiss a mechanism with "acceptable in practice."

*Exercises: form/numeric (word band, ≥3 properties with units) · prohibition (no "acceptable in practice") · presence (HAZ, fracture mechanics, inspection)*

---

## 7. Damage stability of a vessel after flooding

**`naval-damage-stability`**

A 118 m coastal RoRo ferry with a 2,900 t displacement carries vehicles on two decks with a 6.2 m freeboard to the bulkhead deck. Damage is assumed as a 12 m × 4 m breach at the waterline amidships on the starboard side, with a permeability of 0.85 for the vehicle space and 0.95 for the machinery space. Cross-flooding arrangements exist but are untested. Establish the survival condition using the deterministic approach, then state whether the vessel would meet a probabilistic assessment and why the two can disagree. Give the residual freeboard and heel after flooding, the cross-flooding time and its effect on the worst intermediate stage, and the operational restrictions that follow. Identify the scenario in which the vessel survives the final condition but capsizes in the intermediate one. At least 1,300 words, exactly three scenarios, and must contain the damage-stability check explicitly.

*Exercises: form (word floor, 3 scenarios) · must-contain (stability check) · presence (permeability, cross-flooding, intermediate stage)*

---

## 8. Thermal runaway propagation in a battery pack

**`battery-propagation`**

A 78 kWh lithium-ion pack uses prismatic cells at 3.65 V and 280 Ah, arranged 8s, in a sealed aluminium enclosure with no active cooling between modules. A single-cell thermal runaway releases roughly 1.1 MJ over 90 seconds with peak vent-gas temperatures above 600 °C. The pack sits 120 mm below a passenger floor. Design the containment strategy: whether propagation can be prevented or must be managed, the inter-cell barrier material and thickness you would specify and the property that governs the choice, the vent path that keeps combustible gas below its lower flammability limit inside the enclosure, and the detection that warns occupants before the enclosure breaches. Give the propagation time estimate if no mitigation is added and the arithmetic behind it. The design must not claim the pack is "inherently safe" under any condition. Between 1,000 and 1,250 words.

*Exercises: prohibition (no "inherently safe") · form/numeric (word band, propagation estimate) · must-contain (propagation time) · presence (LFL, vent path, detection)*

---

## 9. Shielding design for a hot cell

**`radiological-shielding`**

A shielded cell will handle a 3.7 × 10¹³ Bq cobalt-60 source and a 1.85 × 10¹⁴ Bq iridium-192 source for non-destructive testing. The occupied area outside the wall is a controlled corridor occupied 6 hours per day; the design target is 7.5 µSv/h during occupancy. The wall is currently 1.20 m of ordinary concrete at 2.35 g/cm³. Establish whether the existing wall is adequate for each source, give the required additional thickness if not, and state the tenth-value-layer arithmetic for both. Address the scatter from the corridor's far wall and the skyshine above the roof. Identify the occupational dose that the design permits over a year at the target rate and state whether it is acceptable. Under 1,200 words, exactly two sections, and must contain the tenth-value-layer calculation explicitly.

*Exercises: form (word cap, 2 sections) · must-contain (TVL calculation) · presence (scatter, skyshine, annual dose)*

---

## 10. Lyophilisation cycle for a biologic

**`pharma-lyophilization`**

A 4.2 mL fill of a 28 mg/mL protein formulation must be lyophilised at a 12,000-vial batch scale. The formulation has a measured collapse temperature of −28 °C, a glass transition of −31 °C, a eutectic-free amorphous matrix, and a vial heat-transfer coefficient of 2.1 × 10⁻³ cal/cm²·s·°C. The cake must reconstitute in under 90 seconds and hold a residual moisture between 0.5% and 1.5%. Design the cycle: the freezing protocol and its effect on ice morphology, the primary drying shelf temperature and chamber pressure with the sublimation-rate derivation, the secondary drying endpoint and how you verify it, and the in-process controls that stop a batch before it is lost. Give the primary drying duration and the arithmetic behind it. State what you would do if the batch showed collapse at hour 6. Between 1,250 and 1,500 words; must include ≥3 distinct numeric derivations; must not cite a platform cycle as the reason for a parameter.

*Exercises: form/numeric (word band, ≥3 derivations) · prohibition (no platform-cycle appeal) · presence (collapse temperature, sublimation rate, residual moisture)*

---

## 11. Remediating salinised agricultural soil

**`agri-soil-salinity`**

A 420-hectare block has a root-zone electrical conductivity of 9.4 dS/m, a sodium adsorption ratio of 18, and a water table 1.1 m below the surface with measured salinity of 22 dS/m. The profile is a silty clay loam with a saturated hydraulic conductivity of 2.4 mm/h. Irrigation water is available at 1.8 dS/m and 0.9 ML per hectare per season. Establish whether the block can be returned to production, derive the leaching requirement, state the amendment dose, and give the drainage that the scheme requires and how you would dispose of it. Identify the failure mode that would leave the block saltier than it started, and the single measurement that would tell you the scheme was not working. Give the time to reach the target salinity. Between 1,150 and 1,400 words, exactly four phases, and must contain the leaching and sodicity balance.

*Exercises: form (word band, 4 phases) · must-contain (leaching balance) · presence (SAR, hydraulic conductivity, drainage)*

---

## 12. Treating PFAS in a municipal supply

**`water-pfas-treatment`**

A 42 ML/d municipal plant draws from a river with a measured sum of PFAS at 240 ng/L, dominated by short-chain species. The regulatory limit is 4 ng/L for the sum of four named compounds and the plant must comply within 18 months. Raw water quality varies: dissolved organic carbon swings between 2 and 9 mg/L and turbidity spikes after rain. Design the treatment train: the process you select and the species it does and does not remove, the spent-media handling and its cost driver, the pilot programme that would de-risk the full-scale design, and the monitoring that proves compliance rather than assuming it. Give the mass balance for the media changeout interval. Identify the failure mode that a well-designed train will still exhibit after a heavy-rain event. At most 1,200 words; must contain the media mass balance; must not use the word "simply."

*Exercises: prohibition (banned word, lexical) · form/numeric (word cap) · must-contain (mass balance) · presence (DOC, media changeout, monitoring)*

---

## 13. Moisture in a building envelope

**`building-moisture`**

A cold-climate building with an exterior wall of brick veneer, a drained cavity, 100 mm of mineral wool, and an interior vapour barrier has shown interstitial condensation in the sheathing during the second winter. Interior conditions are 22 °C and 40% relative humidity; the 1% January design temperature is −24 °C. The sheathing is oriented strand board and the cladding has a measured air-leakage rate at the base of the cavity. Determine whether the condensation is a vapour-diffusion or an air-transport problem, give the psychrometric calculation that distinguishes them, and design the repair. State the conservative interior condition you would design to and the safety margin the sheathing needs. Identify the intervention that would make the problem worse and explain why it is commonly recommended. Between 1,100 and 1,350 words, exactly three sections, and must contain ≥2 psychrometric calculations.

*Exercises: form (word band, 3 sections, ≥2 calculations) · presence (dew point, vapour barrier, air leakage)*

---

## 14. Tailings storage facility stability

**`geotech-tailings-dam`**

A 68 m raised tailings dam uses upstream construction, holds 24 Mt, and sits above a community of 1,900 people 4.1 km downstream. The impoundment has a phreatic surface 2.8 m below the crest, a measured residual friction angle of 27°, and a design peak ground acceleration of 0.28 g. Construction records for three of the nine raises are incomplete. Establish the factor of safety under static and pseudo-static conditions, state whether the facility meets a recognised standard, and design the monitoring, surveillance and emergency response that the consequence class requires. Give the failure mode you cannot rule out with the data available, and state plainly whether a credible safety case can be made at all on these records. There is a correct answer here that is not a design. Between 1,150 and 1,400 words; must contain the factor-of-safety derivation; must state explicitly if the available data cannot support a conclusion.

*Exercises: form (word band) · must-contain (FoS derivation) · refusal trap (data insufficiency is the correct answer) · presence (phreatic surface, residual friction)*

---

## 15. Assessing a pipeline with detected cracks

**`pipeline-crack-assessment`**

A 610 mm diameter, 9.5 mm wall natural-gas transmission line built in 1978 has had 41 crack-like features detected by in-line inspection, with depths between 8% and 31% of wall thickness and lengths between 12 and 88 mm. The line operates at 68 bar with a maximum allowable operating pressure of 74 bar, and pressure cycles 4 to 11 times daily with a 38% cycle ratio. There is no in-line inspection history before 2019. Establish the remaining life for the deepest feature, state whether the line can stay at current pressure, and design the re-inspection interval and the pressure restriction if one is required. Give the crack-growth calculation and the inspection-technology qualification that the sizing accuracy depends on. State the one input that would most change the answer. Between 1,200 and 1,450 words; must contain the remaining-life calculation; must not present a probabilistic result without naming the method and its calibration.

*Exercises: form/numeric (word band) · must-contain (remaining life) · prohibition (no uncalibrated probabilistic claim) · refusal trap (sizing-accuracy dependence)*

---

## 16. Avoidance of singularities in a manipulator

**`robotics-manipulator`**

A six-axis industrial arm with 1.8 m reach performs a 900 mm straight-line weld at 12 mm/s, with the tool passing within 140 mm of the wrist singularity and the arm's condition number rising from 4 to over 400 near the path's midpoint. The controller switches to joint interpolation if the commanded Cartesian velocity exceeds what the joints can deliver, which would break the weld geometry. Joint limits are ±170° on the three primary axes. Design the trajectory: the condition-number threshold you would maintain, the path offset or wrist reorientation that avoids the singularity, the velocity profile that stays inside joint limits through the entire path, and the detection that halts the move before the controller switches modes. Give the condition number at the worst point after your redesign and the joint velocities there. Under 1,150 words, exactly two sections, and must contain the condition-number calculation.

*Exercises: form (word cap, 2 sections) · must-contain (condition number) · presence (singularity, joint limits, mode switch)*

---

## 17. Laser damage threshold in an optical train

**`photonics-laser-damage`**

A pulsed laser delivers 1064 nm, 12 ns pulses at 40 J/cm² to a fused-silica window, followed by two lenses and a frequency-doubling crystal. The window's measured laser-induced damage threshold is 28 J/cm² for a 12 ns pulse at 1064 nm under uncompromised conditions, and the manufacturer's specification is materially higher. Surface contamination is present on one lens and the beam has a 3% spatial ripple that creates local hot spots. Establish whether the train survives continuous operation, give the fluence at each optic and the margin at the worst point, and specify the cleaning, handling and beam-conditioning that restores margin. State the mechanism that fails first and the evidence you would need to distinguish it from a different one. Identify which optic fails if the crystal's conversion efficiency drops 15%. Between 1,050 and 1,300 words; must contain the fluence calculation; must not describe any component as "widely available" or "standard."

*Exercises: prohibition (banned phrases, lexical) · form/numeric (word band) · must-contain (fluence calculation) · presence (LIDT, hot spots, conversion efficiency)*

---

## 18. Noise control in an industrial hall

**`acoustics-noise-control`**

A compressor hall with eight machines produces 94 dB(A) at 3 m from the nearest unit, and the boundary fence is 55 m away with a residential receptor 18 m beyond it. The measured spectrum is dominated by 125 Hz and 250 Hz, with a strong 63 Hz component from the largest unit. The applicable night limit at the receptor is 42 dB(A) and there is a 31.5 Hz tone audible inside the nearest dwelling. Design the control scheme to meet the limit, derive the attenuation required per octave band, and specify the engineering measures with the attenuation each contributes. State the measure that treats the tone and why tonal components need separate treatment from the overall level. Give the sound-power-to-pressure derivation that establishes how much must be removed at source. At least 1,250 words; must contain an NR or NC curve target; must specify ≥3 mitigation options each with its attenuation value.

*Exercises: form (word floor, NR/NC target, ≥3 options) · must-contain (NR curve) · presence (octave band, tonal component, sound power)*

---

## 19. Thermal process validation for a canned product

**`food-thermal-process`**

A low-acid canned product in 400 g cans must receive a scheduled process that achieves commercial sterility. The target organism has a D₁₂₁ of 0.55 minutes and a z-value of 9.4 °C. The retort comes up to temperature in 6.5 minutes and the product's slowest-heating point lags the retort by a measured fh of 34 minutes; j is 1.4. Establish the process time that delivers an F₀ of 6 minutes at the cold point, the lethality that the come-up contributes, and the critical factors that must be controlled and recorded. State how you would validate the process in a retort rather than in a laboratory, and what would invalidate the validation. Give the F₀ calculation and the temperature distribution that must be demonstrated. Identify the deviation that would require a recall rather than a rework decision. Between 1,150 and 1,400 words; must contain the F₀ calculation; must not use "commercially sterile" without stating the lethality the term assumes.

*Exercises: prohibition (no undefined "commercially sterile") · form/numeric (word band) · must-contain (F₀ calculation) · presence (D-value, z-value, cold point)*

---

## 20. Smoke management in an atrium

**`fire-smoke-atrium`**

A nine-storey office building has a 32 m atrium open to the full height, with a 5.4 m² design fire on the ground floor at 1.8 MW and a growth time constant of 420 seconds. The building is sprinklered but the atrium is outside the sprinkler coverage. The egress route crosses the atrium floor and the top floor has a 30 m travel distance to the exit. Design the smoke management system: whether the design is a smoke-filling or a smoke-clearance approach and why, the smoke layer descent calculation at the moment egress completes, the exhaust rate required, and the makeup air path. State the tenability criteria you are designing to for visibility and temperature. Identify the condition under which the system fails despite being correctly sized. At most 1,200 words, exactly three sections, and must contain the smoke-layer descent calculation.

*Exercises: form (word cap, 3 sections) · must-contain (smoke layer descent) · presence (design fire, tenability, makeup air)*

---

## Design notes

**Twenty domains, no two adjacent:** orbital mechanics, genomics, structural seismic, power systems, process safety, metallurgy, naval architecture, battery safety, radiological protection, pharmaceutical manufacturing, soil science, water treatment, building physics, geotechnical, pipeline integrity, robotics, photonics, acoustics, food science, fire engineering.

**De-correlated from v1 deliberately.** v1 could be solved by someone who knew operations. This set cannot be solved by someone who knows one thing. **If the harness has a domain-general reasoning capability, this is where it shows; if it has learned software-operations patterns, this is where that stops working.**

**Constraint shapes, deliberately varied:**

| Shape | Count | Items |
|---|---|---|
| Word *floor* (a minimum) | 4 | 3, 7, 14, 18 |
| Word *cap* (a maximum) | 6 | 2, 4, 5, 9, 12, 16, 20 |
| Word *band* | 10 | 1, 6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19 |
| Section or phase count | 9 | 1, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 16, 20 |
| Mandatory calculation | 14 | 1, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 |
| Derivation *count* (≥N) | 4 | 2, 3, 10, 18 |

**Prohibitions, split by class:**

| Class | Items | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Lexical** (banned words/phrases) | 4, 12, 17 | The easy branch — the marker vocabulary should reach these |
| **Semantic** (must not cite X as justification; must not claim Y) | 2, 3, 6, 8, 10, 15, 19 | **The hard branch.** "Must not cite a platform cycle as the reason for a parameter" is about *use*, not containment. The marker cannot see it |

**Refusal traps, and they are the point of the set:** items **12**, **14**, **15** have a correct answer that is *not a design* — the data cannot support the conclusion. `14` is explicit: *"there is a correct answer here that is not a design."* **A harness that generates a confident safety case for a dam with incomplete construction records has failed, not succeeded**, and nothing in the current test suite would catch that.

**Cost:** if v1's pair (items 2 and 7) ran at $0.80 for two, twenty items — several of which will escalate rather than complete — is plausibly **$4 to $12** at current prices. Worth sizing the envelope before starting rather than discovering it.

# technical-set-v3 — format-randomised

**Set:** `evals/scenarios/technical-set-v3`
**Date:** 2026-09-26
**What changed from v2:** same twenty domains, but the **presentation is deliberately randomised**. In v1 and v2 every item was a prose brief with a constraints tail — one template, twenty times. A harness that learned that template would score well on it and learn nothing. Here the constraints appear in a header block, a trailing appendix, mid-sentence, as inequalities, as words, as negative imperatives, as questions, as dialogue, or not at all. **One item (1) is the classic template and is the control.**

**Critical usage note first, because it is a correctness issue:** the format labels below are **metadata for a human reader**. They must be **stripped before the item is loaded as a scenario** — if the planner sees "HEADER-BLOCK CONSTRAINTS" it learns the shape instead of meeting it.

---

## 1 · CLASSIC PROSE + TRAILING TAIL *(the control)*

**`v3-deorbit`**

A 1,240 kg satellite in a 780 km sun-synchronous orbit requires disposal under a post-mission disposal rule. Remaining hydrazine is 38 kg and the delta-v budget is 148 m/s, of which 11 m/s is reserved for attitude control during disposal. Cross-sectional area is 6.8 m² and the ballistic coefficient is 78 kg/m². Atmospheric density at that altitude is highly variable and solar flux is currently rising. Derive the achievable orbit lowering, state the re-entry interval with its uncertainty, identify whether a controlled or uncontrolled re-entry is achievable, and quantify the casualty-risk driver if disposal underperforms. State which assumption dominates the uncertainty and how the plan changes if solar activity falls.

Deliverable: a written disposal plan, 1,100–1,350 words, exactly three sections, including a mass-and-delta-v budget table.

---

## 2 · FIELDED TICKET

**`v3-variant-calling`**

```
RISK:          HIGH
CLASS:         CLINICAL REPORTING
SUBMITTED:     2026-09-26
SAMPLE:        WGS tumour/normal pair
COVERAGE:      tumour 85x | normal 42x
PURITY:        34% +/- 6%
DUPLICATION:   18%
BATCHES:       2 (distinct error profiles)
KNOWN ISSUE:   strand bias at 0.4% of positions (library lot)

DESCRIPTION
Need a somatic variant set fit for a clinical report. The known
strand-bias artefact is in a library-prep lot and must not reach
the report, but low-allele-fraction true variants must survive.

ACCEPTANCE
- minimum evidence thresholds derived FROM PURITY, not assumed
- filtering that removes the artefact and keeps low-AF variants
- orthogonal validation strategy + the fraction it must validate
- reporting thresholds a clinician can act on
- expected false positives at the chosen threshold, with arithmetic

WHAT WE DO NOT WANT
A threshold justified by pointing at a published pipeline.

LIMIT: 1,400 words maximum. Show at least four separate derivations.
```

## 3 · EMAIL

**`v3-seismic-retrofit`**

> **From:** Facilities Director, Regional Health Authority
> **To:** Structural Engineering (commissioned)
> **Subject:** Hospital wing — what can we actually do
>
> We have a four-storey RC moment frame, 1962, hospital wing. It has to stay operational while anything happens to it. Non-ductile detailing throughout, fundamental period reads 0.68 s, and the base shear we computed is 41% of what the current code asks for. Plan is 32 m by 18 m, floor-to-floor 3.6 m.
>
> I need to see at least two retrofit strategies compared. I need to know what performance level and drift limit you are actually designing to, not a generic one. And I need to know whether the existing foundation can take the increased overturning — if it can't, say so early, because that changes everything above it.
>
> One thing I want from you specifically: tell me the failure mode that no amount of strengthening the superstructure will fix. If there is one, I'd rather hear it now.
>
> Length: 1,200–1,450 words, and I want at least 1,250. Two figures exactly. State plainly that a drift check governs the design.
>
> And please don't hand me something described as "proven" unless you can name the evidence for it.

## 16 · GLOSSARY FIRST

**`v3-manipulator`**

**Terms as used here**

- **Condition number** — the ratio expressing how close the Jacobian is to singular at a posture.
- **Wrist singularity** — a configuration where two joint axes align and a Cartesian degree of freedom is lost.
- **Joint interpolation** — motion commanded in joint space; the tool path is not controlled.
- **Mode switch** — the controller's change from Cartesian to joint interpolation when demanded velocity exceeds joint capability.

**Situation.** A six-axis arm of 1.8 m reach performs a 900 mm straight-line weld at 12 mm/s. The tool passes within 140 mm of the wrist singularity. Condition number rises from 4 to above 400 near the path midpoint. Joint limits are ±170° on the three primary axes. A mode switch would break the weld geometry.

**Required.** The condition-number threshold to maintain. The path offset or wrist reorientation that avoids the singularity. The velocity profile that stays inside joint limits throughout. The detection that halts the move before the controller switches modes. The condition number at the worst point **after** redesign, and the joint velocities there. Under 1,150 words, exactly two sections, condition-number calculation included.

## What this set is, and what it is not — stated in the same section as the result, as the repo requires

**It is a coverage instrument.** Twenty formats, twenty domains, one control. **Any pass rate computed over it is a rate over a chosen set and licenses nothing about real objectives.**

**It carries a confound that v1 and v2 did not, and it must be named before the set is run.** A failure here has four possible causes and the score alone cannot distinguish them:

| Cause | Where it would live |
|---|---|
| The **planner** produced unusable criteria from a malformed brief | `plan.success_criteria` |
| The **classifier** could not read criteria phrased as inequalities or words | `criteria_addressed` shape |
| The **solver** could not answer the technical question | the deliverable |
| The **format** defeated the parser before any of the above | graph loading, phase input |

**Item 19 exists to make the fourth distinguishable** — a brief with genuinely missing values. The correct behaviour is to **escalate or ask**, not to invent a D-value of "0.55ish." If 19 completes with a confident thermal process, that is a fabrication finding, not a pass — and it is the highest-value single observation in the set.

**Per-item instrumentation is required for this set to mean anything:** the run record must carry, per item, the criteria the planner generated, the shape each was classified as, and the abstention count. Without that, a low score is unattributable and the exercise buys nothing.

**Cost:** unknown and probably wide. v1's pair ran $0.80 for two. Several items here will escalate rather than complete, and escalation is 70–78% of hard-trace spend. **Size the envelope before starting.** If a full run is too expensive, **run items 1, 11, 17, 19 and 20 first** — that is one control, two numeric-format variants, one refusal trap and one all-prohibition item, and it would tell you whether format variance is a real axis at a fraction of the cost.

Now it's fully pinned down, and it settles the whole thread. Here's the mechanism, from the code:

The fixer is implement, re-run on the engineering tier. After validate goes red, the loop returns to the implement node (qwen3-235b) and it regenerates the implementation. And critically — it is not flying blind. On each re-run the implement prompt is fed a complete diagnosis (phases.py):

- the verbatim red_cause: "PREVIOUS ITERATION FAILED. Cause: {red_cause}. Address this specific failure in your implementation."
- the full per-criterion evidence — every criterion validate judged, not just the one it named (this was a deliberate fix; the feedback used to be lossy)
- the unmet criteria quoted verbatim (Ruling D21: "recovery must carry the failure forward")
- the domain-review findings

So the loop hands the fixer a precise, complete diagnosis: "κ=17.99 violates your stated 17 threshold — fix it." And it still couldn't.

That's the answer to the whole line of questioning: the fix pipeline is information-complete — it's already been hardened by rulings so nothing gets dropped. The bottleneck is not feedback plumbing and not the validator. It's that the thing performing the fix is the same non-reasoning model, regenerating the whole implementation from a contradiction it can't reason through. Told "your number breaks your own rule," a non-reasoning model rewrites everything and tends to re-introduce the same class of inconsistency.

So, concretely, what would change the fix:
- Not a smarter validator (it already caught it and the diagnosis already reaches the fixer).
- Not better feedback wiring (already complete).
- The fixer needs reasoning. The implement node is where the repair happens, so completion on hard numeric problems requires a reasoning model there — which is the tier_when move: route implement/engineering to a reasoning model on high/critical risk, keep non-reasoning qwen3-235b for the routine bulk. That's the single change that targets the actual bottleneck.
- Or accept that some of these correctly block — a diagnosed, honest block on a genuinely hard contradiction is the harness working, not failing.

But there's one gap in "the fixer is information-complete," and if it's real it's a bigger bottleneck than the model.

**Your list of what implement receives is: red_cause, per-criterion evidence, unmet criteria verbatim, domain findings. It does not include the previous artifact.**

If that's the case, the implement node is not editing its prior implementation — it is **generating a fresh one from a diagnosis.** Those are different tasks. "Here is your artifact, κ=17.99 on line 40, your threshold is 17, fix that line" is a local edit. "Here is a diagnosis of a failure in something you didn't just write" is a regeneration, and a regeneration will produce a new artifact with *new* inconsistencies. That is exactly the "re-introduces the same class" behaviour you're describing — and it would happen to a reasoning model too, just less often.

So before the model swap, one question worth one grep: **does the implement prompt carry the prior implementation?** If it doesn't, you have two independent changes and the reasoning-model one may be masking the other.

**The test that discriminates is cheap and you already have the setup.**

Same two items, same everything, one change: route implement to a reasoning model on the high-risk gate. Three outcomes, all informative:

- **Solves it** → the non-reasoning implementer was the binding constraint. The `tier_when` move is validated, and you now know the fixer class.
- **Still blocks, but differently** → the fix shape is wrong, not the model. That points at the prior-artifact question, or at regeneration-vs-patch.
- **Still blocks identically** → the criteria may be unsatisfiable as generated, and the interesting question moves upstream to the planner. That's a different project.

The third outcome is the reason to run it rather than reason about it. It's the one that would redirect you away from the implement tier entirely.

**On cost, one thing to expect:** if implement goes premium on high/critical, the run cost profile changes, and escalation is already 70–78% of hard-trace spend. `tier_when` is the right control — but measure the new profile, because "reasoning at implement" and "reasoning at escalation" may both fire on the same run and the composition will differ from either alone.

**And your second option is right, with one distinction.** A diagnosed honest block is the harness working. But **honest and correct are not the same**, and the block reason can't tell you which. Right now the block is honest — it names the bound and the failure — and you don't know whether it's correct, because the fixer was underserved. That's precisely what the test above resolves: if it blocks with a reasoning implementer, the block is correct. If it solves, the block was honest about an under-capability, which is still a good terminal but a different claim.

Neither outcome is a failure. Both are the harness reporting something true about itself.

- Still blocks → now V2 is warranted and un-confounded, because you've held the prompt shape fixed.

Confirmed, and the inversion is right. V2-only would have been a confounded experiment, and the Fable datapoint genuinely doesn't separate them — it shows a reasoning model clears the class, not that reasoning was necessary given a patch-shaped prompt. V1 first is cheaper, cleaner, and it's the one that, if it works, saves you the entire cost-profile shift.

**One refinement, because without it V1 is a third variable rather than a test.**

The coder's phrasing — *"pass the prior summary into implement"* — describes adding a parameter. That is not the same experiment as patch-vs-regenerate, because the prompt currently says *"Produce the implementation for the following plan. This is iteration N."* A model shown its prior artifact under an instruction to **produce** will still produce. It will produce something that resembles what it was shown, but it is regenerating, not editing — and a failure under that condition would tell you nothing about whether patching works.

**V1 must be both: the artifact passed verbatim, and the instruction changed from produce to revise** — preserve what the criteria judged correct, change only what the diagnosis and the unmet criteria require. Otherwise you've tested "regenerate while seeing your prior output," which is neither arm of the question and would send you to V2 on a false negative.

Two other things the design should carry:

**The regression watch is the `-049` lesson.** Rework turned a green build red on `consistency`. A revision instruction that over-preserves, or an edit that breaks a different criterion, is the failure mode to instrument — *no criterion that was green goes red* belongs in the acceptance.

**Prompt-size delta is a real cost.** The artifact is prose; adding it every iteration grows input tokens on every pass. Report the delta, because on a long artifact the loop's cost rises even when it converges faster.

# Two near-future ideas, ordered

**UI first, batch second** — and the reason is not that the UI is cheaper, it's that they compound differently. At your current volumes ($0.06–$0.80 a run, ~$6/day) the frugality lever is small and bounded. The observability lever compounds: **every refutation in this session was diagnosed by reading a trace by hand**, and the last four were each a manual dig. A watchable surface makes the next twenty runs cheaper to understand than this one was.

Neither is the critical path — V1/V2 is. These are the two things worth building *after* it, and in this order.

---

## 1. The watchable surface

**The key architectural fact: this is a rendering problem, not an instrumentation problem.** The harness has something most agent systems don't — a **typed graph** where every transition is a discrete, structured event with a named node, a tier, a verdict, and a fold state. The unit record already carries cost, calls by tier, per-criterion shape, abstentions, `providers_by_function`, `stop_reason`, and `rejections_by_tier`. **The data to make this watchable mostly exists.** What's missing is emission and rendering, not measurement.

<details open>
<summary><strong>The three surfaces, and the one that matters most</strong></summary>

**A. The run view — where it is now.** The graph as a live path: which node executing, which pending, which skipped. Each node labelled with its tier and, as it completes, its cost and latency. This is the least interesting surface but the most obviously expected.

**B. The call ledger — what it cost.** Per tier: calls, tokens in/out, latency, serving id. Roll-up against the envelope. You already have this per-run; live is the delta.

**C. The criteria × iterations grid — and this is the one worth building.**

The natural unit of display in this harness is **not the run, it is the iteration.** Put criteria on one axis and iterations on the other, and colour each cell by verdict — green, red, abstained, empty seat.

That single view makes three things visible that currently require reading JSONL:

| What it shows | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Convergence** — red cells going green down the column | the thing the product promises |
| **Oscillation** — the same criterion red every iteration | the `κ=17.99` class, visible at a glance |
| **Regression** — green at iteration 1, red at iteration 2 | **the `-049` failure mode**, which cost a run and was found by reading a trace |

You spent a week finding regressions by reading traces. This is a grid.

</details>

**What's actually missing, and it's two things:**

**1. Event emission during the run.** The run is likely synchronous inside a request, and the unit record is written at the end. To watch live you need per-node events as they happen — either SSE from the detail endpoint or an append-only event log the dashboard polls. **This is the same problem as `/api/workflows/sync` blocking**, and `-012` (human surface) was scoped and never executed. It's the real work here.

**2. The "thinking" is not preserved anywhere.** The harness captures *verdicts*, not reasoning. Whether you can show reasoning at all depends on whether your serving exposes it — some reasoning models return a reasoning field, some return only the final content, and some return a **post-hoc summary that is not the actual chain**. That last case is a real hazard: **a displayed rationale that reads as the reasoning but isn't would be a defect in the instrument, not a feature** — the same class as every guard we deleted. If you show thinking, it must be labelled as what it is.

Two consequences worth knowing before you plan for it: reasoning tokens are usually **billed as output**, so displaying thinking raises cost; and storing full reasoning across many runs is a data-volume decision, not just a display one.

**One security caveat that is not small.** Auth is currently open by default. A live view that streams prompts, artifacts and reasoning to anyone who hits port 8100 is a **strictly larger exposure than the current API** — you'd be publishing the inputs and intermediate state, not just the results. The UI and auth-on-by-default are the same decision, and doing the UI first without it would be a regression in posture.

---

## 2. Batch input/output for frugality

**The sharp constraint: the harness's core value is a convergent loop, and batch is inherently non-interactive.** A batched request is submitted and waited on; it cannot participate in the next iteration of a loop that needs its answer. So batch cannot touch `implement`, `validate`, `coverage`, or any judge — those are in the loop.

**That gives the design: batch is a per-node property, not a per-run property.**

```yaml
- id: research_lookup
  kind: ai
  tier: research
  latency_tolerant: true     # ← the new attribute
```

The graph is YAML data, so this fits the architecture exactly: you mark the nodes that don't need to respond to feedback, and those can submit to a batch tier. Candidates: `research`, `search`, context assembly, and possibly `triage` — anything whose output feeds a *later* iteration rather than shaping the current one.

Three things that make this harder than it looks:

- **Batch endpoints typically have a latency floor measured in minutes to hours.** That may exceed your scenario timeout. The 600s wall-clock lesson applies directly: a batch node needs a declared budget, and the loop must emit a terminal if it's missed.
- **Batch availability is narrower than interactive.** Not every serving is in a batch endpoint, so `tier_when` would need a batch-capable roster — and you'd be measuring a different set of models than the pinned ones.
- **Losing the ability to re-prompt** means a malformed batch response can't be retried in-loop. It needs a fallback path, which is exactly the thing I'd want a ruling on rather than an attribute.

**But the ordering insight matters more than the mechanism.** The frugality ranks are:

| Rank | Lever | Size |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Don't run at all** — free checks pre-empt paid (already convention 2) | largest, already done |
| **2** | **Don't escalate** — convergence | **70–78% of hard-trace spend** |
| 3 | Batch the latency-tolerant nodes | ~50% on those nodes only |
| 4 | Cache across runs — knowledge store, semantic reuse | depends on overlap |

**Rank 2 dwarfs rank 3.** Escalation is 70–78% of hard-trace spend; batch discounts a subset of the remaining 22–30%. So the honest framing is: **batch is worth building, and it is not the frugality lever** — V1/V2 is. If the goal is cheaper runs, the route is convergence, and batch is a refinement that pays once runs are already converging.

There's a real secondary case for it though, and it's the one I'd lead with: **batch makes large evaluation sweeps affordable.** Running the 20-item technical set at half price on the latency-tolerant nodes is meaningful when the set is 20 scenarios and several escalate. That's an experiment-enabling tool more than a production-cost tool.

---

Both are **product** work and both are **after** the discriminator. I'd resist letting either displace `-081`, because the thing you don't know yet — whether the fix class is prompt-shape or model-class — determines whether V2 shifts your cost profile by a lot, and that changes what batch is even worth.

The sequence I'd suggest: **run `-081` → build the criteria × iterations grid (it's small, it's the debugging instrument for everything after) → auth-on-by-default in the same change → batch as an eval-scale tool, not a production optimisation.**

The grid is the highest-value item in this whole message, and it's the smallest. You already have the data; you're missing one view.

# The tightest bound is telling you the least — and that's the actual finding

I don't have the trace, so this is inferred from what you've stated plus the measured numbers. But the arithmetic is decisive enough to name the mechanism.

## What this run is, read against the numbers you have

`conv_pool_sizing` is the item that **blocked at 42 calls** in the earlier pair. That is the full failure path. `-051` case (c) measured it precisely: **5 build iterations → escalation → 3 recovery iterations = 8 implement calls, 31 total AI calls.**

Now put a premium roster under it:

$$31 \text{ calls} \times 90\text{–}120 \text{ s/call} \approx 2{,}800\text{–}3{,}700 \text{ s} \approx 47\text{–}62 \text{ minutes}$$

Your per-unit timeout is **900 s — 15 minutes.** So the timeout fires at roughly call 8 of 31.

**Three bounds are competing, and they fire in this order:**

| Bound | Value | Fires at | What it reports |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Wall-clock timeout** | 900 s | **~call 8** | *"timed out"* — nothing about the work |
| Per-unit dollar cap | $0.55 | ~call 18 (at ~$0.03/call) | *"spent ceiling"* — names the bound, not the failure |
| Loop iteration bounds | 5 + 3 | ~call 31 | **escalated with a diagnosis** |

**The tightest bound is the one that names least.** That is the whole problem in one line, and it's the same shape as `-049` — where 528 of 600 seconds went into four calls — and the same shape as the "robotics D33-o" run you mention. **Three occurrences. This is no longer an incident, it's the dominant terminal for hard items.**

## This is code, and it's masking the model question

You asked model or code. The honest answer is **both, and they're ordered** — the code issue determines whether you can even see the model issue.

- **The timeout is mis-sized by design.** It was chosen as a wall-clock default, but the loop's real bounds are in *iterations*. For a cheap roster, iterations bind and you get a meaningful terminal. For a premium roster, wall-clock binds and you get an uninformative one. **So the roster choice silently decides whether the run teaches you anything.** That is a code/config defect, not a capability finding.
- **The run is opaque while executing.** Python buffering stdout *and* the JSONL only writing at unit termination means a running unit is unreadable. So "cycling or converging" is currently unanswerable — not hard, unanswerable.

**And here's the sharp part:** this run will spend $0.55 × 2 and likely produce two *"timed out"* records. **You are paying for a result that has been stripped of its content by the budget.** The capability signal — did it converge, did it block with a diagnosis, did the D33 patch shape help — is being destroyed before it reaches you.

## What would have to be true for this to be model

Three things, and none can be checked until the run is visible:

1. **It reaches the failure path and still blocks with a diagnosis** after D33 gives it its own artifact. That would be a genuine capability limit.
2. **Calls are slow because reasoning is happening**, not because a serving is stalling. 1–2 min/call is plausible for reasoning; it's also what a hung retry looks like.
3. **The cycle is progressive** — each iteration a *different* failure — rather than the same failure re-rolling. The second is the regeneration signature; the first is genuine difficulty.

**Without per-call events you cannot distinguish 2 from a stall, or 3 from a loop bug.** That's why the code fix comes first.

## The fixes, ordered

**Fix 1 — per-call events, flushed.** Emit a record as each call completes: node, tier, serving, tokens, latency, verdict, cost-so-far. Line-buffered or unbuffered stdout, and append to the JSONL per event rather than per unit. **This is the same infrastructure the UI idea needs**, so it's not throwaway work — it's the first slice of it. And it turns a 13-minute blind wait into a readable timeline.

**Fix 2 — make the timeout a derived bound, not a default.** Per D25's own logic: a scenario declares a budget *sized to its iterations*. Compute it from the roster's measured latency:

$$\text{timeout} \ge (\text{max build iters} + \text{max recovery iters}) \times \text{measured } p_{50} \text{ latency} \times \text{calls per iteration}$$

Or simpler and safer: **drop wall-clock as the primary bound.** Dollars and calls are the real economic limits; wall-clock is a proxy that misfires on exactly the runs you care about. Keep it as a very generous backstop — hours, not minutes — and let iterations and dollars do the bounding.

**Fix 3 — abort on projection, with a reason.** The runner has measured latency after two calls. It can project the remaining path:

$$\hat{t} = \text{remaining calls} \times \bar{t}_{\text{observed}}$$

If $\hat{t} > \text{budget}$, stop early and record **"projected 31 calls × 95 s = 49 min against a 15 min budget"** — which is a *useful* terminal, unlike a silent timeout. It tells you the budget was wrong rather than the work.

**Fix 4 — name which bound fired, and whether it was intended.** The record should distinguish *"escalated because the loop bound was reached"* from *"timed out before the loop bound could be reached."* The second is a configuration fault and should say so.

## What to do with the run in flight

**Let it finish.** It's bounded and it costs $0.55. Its value is narrow but real: it confirms the failure path is present and it gives you the per-step timings for Fix 2's derivation. **But predict the outcome now so you're not surprised:** it will most likely record *timed out* for unit 1 and start unit 2 from scratch, also likely to time out — unless unit 2 is a different item with a shorter path.

**And the moment it terminates, before anything else:** read whether the path went build → escalation → recovery → escalate, or whether it looped. That single fact separates "the loop is bounded and slow" from "the loop is cycling," and it's the only thing this run can teach you about the model question.

## One thing worth saying plainly

You now have three runs where **the budget, not the problem, decided the outcome.** `-049` at 600 s, robotics D33-o, and this one at 900 s. That is a systematic mis-sizing, and it means your recent evidence about capability is contaminated — every "didn't finish" on a hard item may be the clock rather than the harness. **Fix the bound before running the next hard item, or you'll keep buying uninformative results.**

Short answer: **not for this issue — and the free version of the thing you want already exists.**

## Why it doesn't fix this

Three reasons, and the first is fatal.

**BigQuery isn't real-time.** The problem is you can't see a run *while it's running* — 13 minutes of blind wait, nothing flushed. BigQuery is a batch analytics store; even wired through an event broadcast, the data lands after the fact. It would give you a better postmortem, and you don't have a postmortem problem. You have a liveness problem.

**It doesn't move the bound.** The run is going to time out at 900 s whether or not a log exists. External logging observes the misfire; it doesn't fix the sizing. That's the actual defect.

**And the cost is upside down.** Streamed inserts plus storage would plausibly run more per month than this project spends on models ($6/day, runs at $0.06–$0.80). You'd be buying observability infrastructure that costs more than the thing observed.

## What it *would* fix — a different and real problem

**Independent reconciliation of billable calls.** OpenRouter sees every call that actually left the harness. The harness sees every call it *thinks* it made. Those have diverged here, with receipts: retry events appeared in stderr while both rejection counters read empty, and the meter epoch means pre-`b4cd89f` figures were understated 2.7×–295×.

So the honest framing: **OpenRouter's log is a witness, not an instrument.** It can tell you the harness's accounting is wrong. It cannot tell you what the harness concluded, which node made the call, or whether the loop converged. You'd need both, joined.

**And the join key is the generation id.** That's the cheap bridge, and it belongs in the harness-side per-call event already proposed in `-082` — capture OpenRouter's generation id per call and log it locally. Then the dashboard record and the harness record line up, and you get reconciliation for the cost of one field rather than one service.

## Do this instead, right now, for free

**Read the OpenRouter activity log for the current run.** It requires no setup, no BigQuery, no code. And it would answer the model-vs-code question in about two minutes, because it shows the two things that discriminate:

- **Per-call latency and `finish_reason`** — a call taking 90 s with a large reasoning token count is the model reasoning. A call returning in 2 s with 50 tokens means the wall-clock is going somewhere *else*, and the waste is in code.
- **Call count and repetition** — if the log shows more generations than the harness recorded, you have a retry or accounting bug. If it shows exactly what the harness recorded, the loop is genuinely cycling and the model is the suspect.

That single read separates the two hypotheses. If OpenRouter shows calls at ~90–120 s each with heavy reasoning output, it's the model and the fix is a cheaper roster for the build path or a longer derived budget. If it shows fast calls and the run still takes 13 minutes, something in the harness is stalling between calls, and that's a code bug no logging service would have found either.

## The instinct worth naming

This is the same move as the guards and the taxonomies: **reach for a new instrument in response to a problem, before checking whether the data is already there.** Twice this session the answer was "the information exists, it isn't being surfaced" — the terminal that named the bound but not the criterion, and the credential warning nobody had computed. Both were fixed by *reading better*, not by adding.

The free path — dashboard for diagnosis, generation id for reconciliation, per-call events for liveness — covers all three needs. BigQuery would add a fourth instrument for the one part that isn't the actual problem.

**One caveat on my own confidence:** I don't know precisely what OpenRouter's export integrations currently offer, so I'm reasoning about the capability class rather than the feature list. If their BigQuery path is real-time via webhook and free at your volume, the liveness objection weakens — but the first two reasons stand regardless, because a log doesn't re-size a bound.

I've worked through all twenty rows. **The model-class hypothesis is not supported. This is a context defect and a routing defect, in that order — and both are ours.**

## The numbers

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Calls | 20 |
| Total cost | **$0.201** |
| Input tokens | **877,184** |
| Output tokens | **27,961** |
| Input:output ratio | **31 : 1** |
| Speed range | **2.7 → 157.3 tok/s (58×)** |
| Max TTFT | **75.22 s** |
| Finish reasons recorded | all **`stop`** — no truncation |

## Finding 1 — three calls carry 95% of the context and 66% of the cost

| Time | Input | Output | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 03:24 | 275,559 | 4,260 | $0.0333 |
| 03:31 | 277,612 | 7,288 | **$0.0920** |
| 03:33 | 281,310 | 3,005 | $0.00641 |

$$\frac{834{,}481}{877{,}184} = 95.1\% \text{ of all input tokens in } \frac{3}{20} = 15\% \text{ of calls}$$

**Three calls at ~280k tokens each.** And note their per-token prices — $0.023/M, $0.119/M, $0.323/M — **three different rates, so three different servings.** They are visibly the same call type routed to three providers.

**What 280k tells you:** it is the *opposite* of frugal. Something is filling the window, and 275k–281k clustering so tightly suggests it is being filled *to* a cap rather than sized to need. Either the grounding corpus is genuinely that large — in which case it needs summarising and prompt caching, not re-sending — or context is accumulating across iterations, in which case it needs a window. **You cannot tell which from outside, and that is the first thing to instrument.**

## Finding 2 — speed varies 58× and input size does not explain it

| Population | Input range | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| Slow | 1,054–5,748 | **2.7 – 11.3 tok/s** |
| Fast | 309–6,640 | **60 – 157 tok/s** |

**The input ranges overlap almost completely.** So prompt size is *not* the speed discriminator. Same harness, same loop, same tier — and a call either runs at 5 tok/s or at 130. That is **an unpinned tier drawing different providers inside one run**, which is exactly what §6.1 and §6.11 recorded as having decided two of this project's largest findings.

One call: **TTFT 75.22 s, 957 output tokens at 2.7 tok/s ≈ 354 seconds.** A single call, six minutes, for a thousand tokens.

## Finding 3 — every recorded call completed normally

**All finish reasons say `stop`.** No `length`, no truncation, no empty reply. The models are *answering*. The 58× variance and the six-minute call are not the model failing to reason — they are a serving taking that long.

**This is the discriminator I asked you to read the log for, and it comes back clean:** the lattice is fine, the serving is slow.

<details>
<summary><strong>What this does to my previous hypothesis — I was partly right, partly wrong</strong></summary>

**Right:** the timeout is too short. ~20 calls took ~17 minutes ≈ **51 s/call**. A 31-call failure path at that rate is **~1,580 s ≈ 26 minutes** against a **900 s** budget. The timeout fires around call 18 of 31. Confirmed.

**Wrong:** I attributed the latency to *premium reasoning models being inherently slow*. The log shows **most calls are fast** (60–157 tok/s — that is not a slow reasoning model, that is a fast serving). The wall-clock is eaten by a **minority of calls landing on starved servings**, not by the roster being premium across the board.

**So the fix ordering inverts.** I had said: longer budget, or cheaper roster. Neither is first. **Fix the routing and the context, and the budget may not need to move at all.**

</details>

## The fix hierarchy, by measured size

| # | Fix | Addresses | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Cap and instrument the input context** | 95% of tokens, 66% of cost, and the long TTFTs | **largest** |
| **2** | **Pin the roster per tier** — record which serving answered every call | the 58× speed variance | large, and partly config (G-2/G-3) |
| **3** | **Re-derive the timeout** from the *improved* latency | the 900 s misfire | small, and only after 1 and 2 |
| **4** | Per-call events | makes 1–3 visible next time | enables the rest |

**Note the order matters:** `-082` (per-call events + derived bound) is still right, but **it is now the fourth priority, not the first.** Deriving a timeout from the *current* latency would bake in a serving defect — you would size the budget to accommodate a 354-second call instead of fixing why the call took 354 seconds.

**And the V2 question stays genuinely open.** Nothing in this log shows a model failing to reason through the κ contradiction. It shows calls completing at `stop`, and it shows three enormous prompts. **The D33 patch experiment is still the thing that answers patch-vs-regenerate — and the log now says that on the current setup, its result would be contaminated by serving variance.**

# The order was wrong, and the arithmetic says why

I need to correct my own previous answer before ordering anything, because I conflated two problems that have different fixes — and I put the wrong one first.

## The two problems are not the same problem

| | Cost | Latency |
|---|---|---|
| **Where it lives** | the 3 calls at ~280k input | the 8 calls at 2.7–11.3 tok/s |
| **Share** | 95% of input tokens, 66% of cost | **17% of output tokens, ~85% of wall-clock** |
| **Fix** | cap or cache the context | **serving selection** |

**These barely overlap.** The three expensive calls carry 280k inputs; the slow calls carry **1,054 to 5,748** inputs. The single largest call by input (6,640) ran at **79.8 tok/s — fast.**

So **capping the context will not fix your timeouts.** It fixes cost. The timeouts are a different defect.

## And the latency arithmetic is stark

Eight calls at 2.7–11.3 tok/s produced **4,670 output tokens**. At an average ~6 tok/s:

$$4{,}670 \div 6 \approx 778 \text{ s of a } 900 \text{ s budget} \approx \mathbf{86\%}$$

**Eight calls producing 17% of the output consumed ~86% of the wall-clock.** The timeout fired because ~4,700 tokens were generated on starved servings — not because 31 calls were too many.

**That reframes the whole fix.** If those eight calls had run at the ~80 tok/s their own peers achieved, they'd have taken ~58 seconds instead of ~778. **The 900 s budget would likely have been sufficient as-is.** You don't need a longer timeout. You need the slow calls to not be slow.

## What I can't tell from this log — and it decides the fix

Four explanations fit the variance, and **the log cannot separate them:**

| Hypothesis | Would mean |
|---|---|
| (a) **Different servings**, genuinely different speeds | routing — fix the pin |
| (b) **Provider metrics aren't comparable** — some report output-only, some total | a measurement artifact, not a defect |
| (c) **Same serving, load variance** | capacity, mostly outside your control |
| (d) **Different call types** — a reasoning endpoint vs a fast one | expected; fix is tier assignment |

**(a) is most likely and (b) is the one I'd want ruled out before spending anything**, because a measurement artifact would send you re-pinning servings that are fine.

**And the one fact that discriminates all four is the serving id per call** — which is precisely what the per-call event doesn't currently carry. That's why attribution comes first, and it isn't bureaucracy: without it, every hypothesis above is guesswork.

**Two partial hints, both weak:** the `1,054`-input call appears twice, hours apart, and is slow **both times** (6.0 and 11.3 tok/s) while its peers in the same burst run at 60–157. That pattern — same call slow across occasions, peers fast — points at a **phase-consistent serving**, not random noise. And the `75.22 s` TTFT on one call is hard to explain as a reporting artifact.

## The revised order

| # | Fix | Addresses | Cost | Why here |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Per-call events with phase, tier, serving id** | makes everything below attributable | free | Without it, 1–4 are inferences |
| **2** | **A per-call timeout** | ~354 s single call eating 40% of budget | free | A starving serving should fail in 20 s, not stall for six minutes |
| **3** | **A serving pre-flight** — one cheap call per tier before a run | catches a starved serving for ~$0.001 | ~free | Convention 2's own logic: a free-ish check before an expensive run |
| **4** | **Fix the slow serving** | the 86% | config, owner | The biggest single win on time |
| **5** | **Cap or cache the 280k context** | the 66% of cost | free | Biggest win on money; does *not* fix time |
| **6** | **Re-derive the timeout** | the misfire | free | **Last** — deriving it before 1–4 bakes the defect into config |

**The change from my previous answer:** context capping moves from #1 to #5, and the timeout moves from #3 to #6. **My error was ranking by cost instead of by what actually stops runs.**

## One latent failure in the context data

$$275{,}559 \rightarrow 277{,}612 \rightarrow 281{,}310$$

**Monotonic, growing ~2–4k per occurrence.** A fixed corpus would be constant. Something is accumulating — and if it accumulates per iteration on a loop that reaches 8 iterations, **the next call exceeds the context window and the failure becomes hard rather than slow.**

That needs naming before it bites. Either it's history being re-appended, or a large base (275k) plus small increments.

**And 280k tokens is roughly a 400-page book.** For a pool-sizing question. That is either severe over-retrieval or a bug, and either way it is not "frugal" — which is the stated design goal. **31:1 input:output, $0.20, and no answer is the opposite of the product's whole selling point.**

## More that can be done

- **Check for prompt caching.** If the 275k base is re-sent each iteration and the provider caches prefixes, this is the single largest lever available — it could take the 95% of input tokens near zero. Report whether it's supported and whether the harness requests it.
- **Bound the context *by construction*, not by truncation.** If the retrieval is returning a whole corpus, select rather than send — and record what was dropped.
- **A per-phase latency budget.** Not a global timeout: each phase gets a bound from its own measured p50. Then a starved serving fails alone instead of taking the run down.
- **Reconcile the harness's accounting against this log.** You now have an external witness. **The harness thinks it made N calls; OpenRouter says 20.** If those differ, you have an accounting bug — and this costs nothing to check.
- **Confirm the run boundaries.** I've assumed unit 1 spans 03:16–03:31 and unit 2 starts at 03:33. If that's wrong, the "two similar bursts" reading changes.

## Less that should not be done

- **BigQuery.** It doesn't help liveness, doesn't move the bound, and would cost more than the models.
- **The UI — for now.** Its first requirement (per-call events) is item 1 above, so build that and the UI becomes cheap later. The UI itself doesn't fix anything.
- **V2 / a reasoning model at implement.** This log gives it **zero support** — every call finished `stop`, nothing truncated, nothing empty. The models answered. **Spending on reasoning now would be fixing a serving problem with a model purchase.**
- **More hard scenarios** until attribution exists. Every hard-item result you currently have is contaminated by uncontrolled serving variance — `-049`, robotics D33-o, and this one.
- **Re-deriving the timeout first.** It would size the budget to accommodate a 354-second call that should have taken ten.

## What would make me wrong

**If (b) holds — provider metrics aren't comparable** — then the 58× variance is partly artifact, the slow calls may not be slow, and item 4 (fix the serving) is a fix to a measurement rather than to a serving. **The serving id per call rules this out, and that's why it's item 1.**

**If the failures aren't latency at all** — if the run is also *cycling* through iterations rather than progressing — then speed alone won't fix it, and the D33 patch experiment is still the thing that answers patch-vs-regenerate. I can't tell from this log whether unit 1 was progressing or looping.

**If unit 1 and unit 2 are different scenarios**, then the two similar call bursts I'm reading as structure may be coincidence, and the phase-consistency hint weakens.

---

**One line:** the order was wrong — **cost and latency are separate defects with separate fixes, and the timeouts are caused by eight calls producing 17% of the output in ~86% of the wall-clock, all of them small**, so capping the 280k context fixes money and not time; attribute the calls with the serving id first (it's the only thing that separates routing from a reporting artifact), bound each call individually, fix the slow serving, then cap the context — and re-derive the run timeout **last**, because sizing a budget around a 354-second call that should have taken ten would lock the defect into the config.

# Keeping Qwen changes the target — and it sharpens it

That correction matters more than it looks. If Qwen is the best non-reasoning model you have and time isn't binding, then **my "fix the slow serving" item is withdrawn** — it was a quality-for-speed trade you've already made. And the price arithmetic points at something much more specific than "context is big."

## The price, re-read as a price

$$20 \text{ calls}, \$0.2007, \quad 877{,}184 \text{ in}, \quad 27{,}961 \text{ out}$$

| | Calls | Input tok | Cost | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Three big calls** | 3 (15%) | 834,481 | **$0.13171** | **65.6%** |
| Everything else | 17 (85%) | 42,703 | $0.06903 | 34.4% |

**And your working run — 084 — was 9 calls and $0.06.** So this run isn't expensive because runs are expensive. It's $0.20 because of **one pathology costing ~$0.13.**

**The same call size cost three different prices:**

| Call | Input | Cost | Implied rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 03:24 | 275,559 | $0.0333 | ~$0.121/M |
| 03:31 | 277,612 | **$0.0920** | **~$0.331/M** |
| 03:33 | 281,310 | $0.00641 | ~$0.0228/M |

**Nearly identical input, 14× the cost.** That single call at $0.092 is **46% of the whole run** — and it is the same shape of work as one that cost $0.0064.

**Two independent levers, and they compound:**

$$30{,}000 \text{ tok} \times \$0.0228/\text{M} = \$0.0007 \quad\text{vs}\quad \$0.092 \quad=\quad \mathbf{130\times}$$

Cap the input *and* route that call type to the cheap serving, and the most expensive call in your log becomes free-ish. Across all three: **~$0.13 → ~$0.002, which is a ~65% run-cost reduction.**

## The hypothesis I'd test first, because it explains all three facts

The three calls sit at minutes 8, 15 and 17 of the run — **after the build iterations, in the escalation and recovery window.** Their inputs grow monotonically (275k → 277k → 281k), which fixed content does not do.

That fits §6.10 directly: **escalation is 70–78% of hard-trace spend.** And it fits your own changes: **D21 said recovery must carry the failure forward; D33 said implement must receive its prior artifact. Both added context — and they added it precisely on the expensive path.**

So the likely mechanism: **later phases re-receive accumulated state** — the corpus, prior artifacts, the diagnosis, history — because carrying it forward is what made the loop correct. **The correctness fixes and the cost problem are the same change seen from two sides.**

**I can't confirm this from the log** and I'm not going to assert it. But it predicts something checkable: the 280k calls are escalation/recovery, and their size is base-plus-accumulation rather than a single large retrieval.

## The convergent fix

Capping the input is the rare change that helps **all three** axes at once:

| Axis | Effect | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Price** | ~59% cut | 95% of tokens live there |
| **Latency** | prefill drops with input | a 280k prefill is a large part of the TTFT |
| **Waste** | fewer timeouts | a timed-out run is spend with no deliverable |

**That last one is a price argument you may not have counted.** A run that dies at 900 s produces nothing for its $0.15. **Cost per completed deliverable is the number that matters, and incomplete runs make it infinite.** Shortening the context shortens the prefill, which is what makes the calls long, which is what makes the run hit the wall.

## The other lever, which might be the largest

**If the same ~275k prefix is re-sent each time, prompt caching is the whole answer.** Three sends of the same base is 3× the cost of one; cached, it's roughly one plus deltas. **That is worth more than capping**, and it costs a config line rather than a design change — so check it first.

I can't tell from your log whether it's the same prefix (the sizes differ, which argues either for accumulation or for genuinely different content) or whether your provider offers prefix caching. **Both are one grep.**

## Re-ranked order — price-first, with Qwen kept

| # | Fix | Saves | Cost | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Check prefix caching** | potentially most of the 66% | config | Cheapest intervention, largest possible return |
| **2** | **Locate what produces the 280k** | enables 3 and 4 | free | Code read; no speculation |
| **3** | **Cap by selection, not truncation** | ~59% | free | Record what's dropped — no silent truncation |
| **4** | **Route the big call type to the cheap serving** | up to 14× on those calls | config, owner | G-2/G-3 |
| **5** | **Bound what escalation receives** | ongoing, every hard run | free | Failure-relevant subset, not full state |
| ~~—~~ | ~~Fix the slow serving~~ | — | — | **Withdrawn — Qwen stays** |

**#5 is the structural one.** #1–4 fix *this* pathology; #5 stops the escalation path from re-inflating on every hard run — and hard runs are exactly where you spend.

## What I'd still not do

- **Don't buy reasoning at implement.** The log gives V2 zero support: **every call finished `stop`** — nothing truncated, nothing empty. The models answered.
- **Don't add BigQuery.** Doesn't touch price.
- **Don't re-derive the timeout.** With a bounded context the calls get faster, and you'd be sizing around a pathology.

**One caveat on all of it:** the 14× cost spread might partly be an artifact — if providers report or bill differently, my implied rates are wrong. **That's ruled out by one field: the serving id per call.** Which is why it's still first.
