# The trace is stronger evidence than the log was, and it corrects me twice

The arithmetic is decisive: **758 tokens cannot take 135 s.** At any plausible generation rate that's 7–15 s, so ~120 s per call is not the model — it's waiting. And the trace's per-phase breakdown is internally consistent to within 1 s of the 900 s budget, which the log alone could not give.

**Two of my readings were wrong, and one of them is instructive.**

## The correction: the speed column was measuring backoff

OpenRouter's `Speed` is tokens ÷ total elapsed. If a call waits ~120 s on retries and then produces 758 tokens in ~15 s, the column reports **~5.6 tok/s**. That is not a generation rate — it is a **throughput figure contaminated by retry wait.**

Cross-check, and it's exact:

$$\frac{673\text{ s}}{5\text{ calls}} = 134.6\text{ s/call}, \qquad \frac{758\text{ tok}}{134.6\text{ s}} = \mathbf{5.6\ tok/s}$$

**That lands precisely in the log's slow band (2.7–11.3).** So the slow calls in the log *are* these implement calls — same population, confirmed two ways. And the **75.22 s TTFT** is backoff accruing before the first token.

**So my "58× serving variance / unpinned routing" reading was wrong.** It was **backoff variance** — some calls hit fewer 429s. I noticed the oddity (*"six minutes for a thousand tokens"*) and then accepted the column as a generation speed instead of asking why it looked wrong. The tell was available and I read past it.

## What this does to my earlier proposals

| Proposal | Status |
|---|---|
| "Fix the slow serving" (Qwen) | **Withdrawn** — correctly, and you'd already told me |
| "Context/D33 is the target" for the timeouts | **Refuted** — 4,134-token prompts, iteration 1, D33 adds nothing there |
| "58× serving variance" | **Refuted** — it's backoff |
| **Per-call bound** | **Still right, different reason** — not to catch a slow model, but to catch a **rate-limit crawl**, and fail *named and fast* instead of eating 673 s silently |
| **Re-derive the timeout last** | **Still right** — and now it's "after the rate limit is fixed," which is the same ordering |

The per-call bound survives because it addresses a different thing than I claimed: a 30 s call bound would have turned this into a **fast, named 429 failure** rather than an uninformative timeout. That's a better outcome for the same money.

## The structural point, and it's the one I'd record

**The same cause produced two different failure surfaces:**

| Unit | Manifestation | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| robotics | retries exhausted | **hard 429, fatal, 0 iterations** |
| pool_sizing | 429 → backoff | **crawl → 900 s timeout** |

**One cause, two behaviours, neither one named.** That means the harness's failure surface is **non-deterministic given identical conditions** — whether you get a fast fatal or a slow timeout depends on how many retries happen to succeed. That is worse than either failure alone, because it makes runs uncomparable: you cannot tell a hard scenario from a rate-limited one by looking at the outcome.

**And critically — this was inferable from the run record and wasn't, because retries weren't counted.** `rejections_by_tier` read empty while retry events went to stderr. **Had 429s been counted and attributed per tier, this would have been visible in the trace immediately instead of reconstructed from timing arithmetic.** That's `-030`'s reconciliation gap, directly implicated.

## What the trace does not explain

**The three ~280k-token calls in the log are still homeless.** Engineering ran at 4,134 tokens/call — so those three are **not** engineering, and they still carry 95% of the logged input tokens and 66% of the cost. They're either a different phase (search/grounding), or unit 2. **Exonerating D33 and context for the *timeouts* does not explain them**, and they remain the largest single cost item you have. Worth one lookup, not urgent.

## The fix, with one refinement

Your conclusion is right: **re-pin engineering off DeepInfra.** Two refinements before spending:

**The "own key lifts the shared limit" claim needs checking.** It holds if the limit is per-key on a **shared or free tier**. It does *not* hold if the limit is **per-account** — a new key on the same account can inherit the same ceiling. One question settles it, and getting it wrong means buying a key that changes nothing.

**And I haven't verified that Parasail or Vertex `us-south1` serve the model in question.** That's checkable and I'm not going to confirm it from memory.

**One thing to note about the re-pin:** it re-opens the D33 question cleanly. Once implement is fast, the 900 s budget is no longer suspect — **the timeout was never the problem, it was the symptom.** Which means the D33 verdict test becomes interpretable for the first time.

# Ruling on the proposal: the diagnosis is right, the routing is wrong

**The missing edge is real, and "no new tier" is correct.** But there's one correction that changes the build, and one condition the proposal doesn't have that determines whether the edge works or spins.

## The correction: your three blockers aren't research problems

You named the answer source for each:

| Blocker | You said it's answerable from |
|---|---|
| Container topology | the deployment repo / manifests |
| Current pool settings | the app config or a metrics query |
| App compat (`SET`, `LISTEN`, temp tables) | a codebase grep |

**None of those is the open web.** So if the re-grounding edge routes to the **research/search** tier — which does web lookup — it will re-ask the wrong instrument and fail, exactly as the first pass did. The edge needs to route to a path that can read **the repo, config, a metrics system, and code** — which may be `context`, or may require giving research file access it doesn't have.

**This is a precondition, not a detail.** If research has repo access, your proposal is a wiring change. If it doesn't, the edge alone won't resolve a single one of your three examples.

## The condition it's missing: novelty

**A `plan ↔ grounding` loop is a loop, and loops are how this harness has historically died** — `build_loop` exhaustion, `recovery_loop` being a retry wearing a mechanism's name. The failure mode here is specific and predictable: **re-grounding re-asks the same query, finds the same nothing, spends N rounds, then escalates anyway.**

So the edge needs a termination condition that isn't just a count: **round 2 must ask a question round 1 didn't.** That's checkable — compare the emitted queries; if they're unchanged, stop and escalate rather than burning the round. Without it, "up to N rounds" is a bound around a spin.

## What I agree with, and would record as-is

- **No new tier.** Right, and it's the same call as the Jev decision: a "verification tier" is judging, judging is a check, and the six tiers cover the jobs. Adding a mind is the expensive, wrong move.
- **The escalation order:** re-grounding → declared-assumption-with-basis → human. Right. One addition — the **middle** option must be *labelled and counted*, so you know how often you're assuming rather than resolving. Kimi's autopsies turning "unknown" into a stated assumption with a recompute formula is honest work, and it should appear in the run record as a number, not be invisible.
- **Human input is for what only a human has.** Correct, and it's what `requires_human` already exists for.
- **K2.5 literalism is a grading question, not a grounding one.** Separate, and I'd defer it until the edge is in — otherwise you're changing two things and can't attribute the result.

## The one thing that makes this a ruling and not a hope

**"Targeted re-grounding resolves these unknowns" is a hypothesis.** You have three examples from one night. What you don't know is the *rate* — of the unknowns a plan names, what fraction does a second targeted pass actually resolve, versus deferring to escalation with a round spent?

**So the command builds the edge, and the paid measurement follows it** — pre-registered, on your committed blockers, reporting the resolve rate. **If the rate is low, the honest finding is that the unknowns are genuinely not in your retrievable sources, and the edge is a round-cost for a deferral.** That's worth knowing before it's wired into every hard run.
